prize_parts.citation: for developing empirical methods to estimate demand and market power in differentiated-product industries, and for a framework for analysing dynamic industry evolution

statement.case_for: The Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes approach solved a concrete problem: estimating demand for differentiated products when prices are endogenous and consumer tastes are heterogeneous. It made it possible to measure markups, merger effects and welfare from realistic market data. Before it, empirical work either used restrictive demand systems with implausible substitution patterns or relied on reduced-form price regressions that could not support counterfactuals. The method has been in routine use for about three decades in antitrust and merger review, regulation, trade, health and environmental economics. That is long and varied confirmation of the kind I would want before a prize. The attribution is the cleanest of the candidates I rank highly. The BLP papers are jointly authored by the three named people, and Pakes separately anchors the dynamic-oligopoly and estimation line (Ericson-Pakes and later work). The contribution is also a discovery about how economists can learn about competition from data, not only a statistical tool. It links identification, structural modelling and policy-relevant counterfactuals.
statement.case_against: The three-name cap leaves out Bresnahan and Reiss, whose earlier work on identifying market power and conduct from data is seminal, and Benkard and Levin, who contributed to dynamic estimation. A three-person prize could therefore be seen as crediting the demand-estimation tool while understating the wider empirical-IO programme. The contribution is also largely methodological and concentrated in one subfield. The committee may weigh it against candidates with broader conceptual or societal reach, such as B002 or B038, or against long-overdue foundational theory such as B001. Practical uptake of the dynamic-model estimation line is more mixed than that of demand estimation.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B030 sixth. He accepts Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes as the core of demand estimation, but notes that Bresnahan, Reiss and others are left out. He also questions whether the committee sees this as a methods prize or an applied one, and notes that dynamic-model estimation has had mixed practical adoption. His first place goes to Rubinstein-Wolinsky bargaining.
responses.response: I agree on the dynamic-models point, and it shapes my citation. The weight should rest on demand estimation and on Pakes's conceptual framework for dynamic industries, not on a claim that dynamic structural estimation is now routine. I also accept that Bresnahan's conduct-identification work is a real omission under the three-person cap. I would rather accept that cost than dilute a clear core. I take his first-place case for B001 seriously. The Rubinstein result is canonical and maturity is not in doubt, which is why I list B001 as my first alternative. My remaining difference with him is that bargaining theory sits in a field already prized several times, while structural demand estimation has never been recognised as such.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B041 first, with Melitz as the central contributor and Helpman as co-recipient. He argues that firm heterogeneity reorganised trade theory and measurement, and that Redding's quantitative extensions are later and secondary.
responses.response: I agree that Melitz (2003) is the core and that Redding is a later, more quantitative line. Because I work close to this field, I am wary of letting familiarity raise my view. My reservation is attribution and the size of the gains. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made parallel contributions and are not on the ballot. Helpman's role is also split between B041 and B013, so the committee could face a choice of framing for him. Estimates of the welfare gains from selection also depend on the specification. That is why I rank B041 fourth and list it as an alternative. I do not see it as clearly more settled than BLP, though Hassler's point about two decades of theory, structural estimation and firm-level evidence is a fair one.

responses.point: Boppart ranks Kiyotaki-Moore first. He argues that the collateral-constraint mechanism is a foundation of macro-finance, validated by the 2008 crisis, and that a two-person core avoids the Gertler-Gilchrist attribution problem.
responses.response: The two-person attribution is clean, and three decades of confirmation is a strong maturity case. I ranked it eighth. That reflects my distance from macro-finance and my concern about overlap with the 2022 prize and Bernanke's accelerator work, not a view that the mechanism is weak. I would qualify one point. Direct empirical identification of the collateral channel is still contested, as several colleagues noted in their own uncertainties, and that matters for a prize built on a mechanism. I do not think the 2022 overlap is disqualifying. My view is that the case is strong but not stronger than B030's, whose methods have been tested across many industries.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B038 first. She argues that it combines new data with an explanatory framework, that more than fifteen years of replication have made the research design standard, and that the work has had wide impact on research and policy.
responses.response: The empirical design is credible and the societal reach is broad, and I do not dispute either. I ranked B038 seventh for three reasons. First, the shift-share identification strategy remains under scrutiny, and the size and persistence of the effects are still debated. Second, the task-based framework owes a good deal to scholars outside the credited names, so the trio's credit is clean only for the China-shock strand. Third, the 2024 prize touched adjacent themes on technology. I would be more comfortable if the committee defined the achievement as the China-shock evidence alone, since combining the two strands makes the prize rationale harder to state. She also raised dependence on restricted data for B002, which is a fair concern for that candidate too.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat structural demand estimation and dynamic industry models as one coherent achievement or as two lines with different maturity and uptake.

How to weigh Bresnahan and Reiss. Crediting only Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes may under-represent the empirical-IO programme, and I have not resolved whether a different three-person set would be more defensible.
Whether a methods-centred prize should rank behind candidates that offer a substantive discovery about the economy, given how colleagues have framed their criteria.

My ranking of B030 first may partly reflect familiarity with IO and trade. The opening shows only three members ranked it, and I cannot tell whether that reflects a real merit judgement or limited familiarity outside the field.
Whether my low ranking of B012 and B038 would change if I had more field expertise in macro-finance or labour.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal-level connection is apparent from the supplied profile. None of the credited names on the shortlisted ballots is among my listed co-authors (Asplund, Steen, Ulsaker, Grönqvist, Wilander, Syverson, Goldstein). I work in industrial organisation and international trade, which is adjacent to B030 and B041, so I treat my familiarity as a disclosure and not as evidence of merit. I co-authored a 2026 paper with committee chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen, but this is not a connection to any candidate. My spouse's public political role (Magdalena Andersson) is noted as a public fact only, and I see no bearing on any shortlisted candidate.
